title: Enjambment, Caesura and Tone
welcome_lead: Punctuation, line-break, voice — examine the subtler tools that build a poem's atmosphere.
meta_desc: Enjambment, caesura, tone and voice in poetry at A-Level English Literature.
final_note: You can now describe a poem's breath — its breaks, its pauses and the voice that carries it.

concepts.def: Continuation of a sentence beyond the line end, creating momentum and surprise.
Line whose sense closes with the line break, often signalled by punctuation.
A pause within a line, often medial, marked by punctuation; alters rhythm and emphasis.
The poem's emotional colouring — ironic, elegiac, jubilant — emerging from diction and rhythm.
The implied speaker of the poem, distinct from the historical poet (persona).
Word choice — Latinate vs Anglo-Saxon, concrete vs abstract — that shades meaning.

walkthroughs.body_html:
An enjambed line pushes meaning forward. Wordsworth's And I have felt / A presence... delays revelation, building suspense across the break.

End-stopping anchors meaning; enjambment destabilises it.

A caesura — often a dash, comma or full stop mid-line — creates a heartbeat pause.

Pope's heroic couplets use caesurae to balance halves of a line: To err is human; — to forgive, divine.

Tone emerges from diction, image and rhythm. The same scene rendered in clipped monosyllables versus lavish Latinate vocabulary produces opposite tonal effects.

Persona poems (Browning's monologues) further complicate tone — the speaker may be unreliable.
